archetype.name: Point Guard (screen-heavy, legs quiet)
archetype.definition: In 2026 Nix is a quick-release distributor who lives behind the line and under 10 air yards, protected well but rarely pushing the ball to the sticks, and the rushing that used to rescue his drives has disappeared.

report.headline: The legs vanished and the passing went short: Nix is surviving, not driving.
report.take:
Nix came into his third season with a clear identity. He was a solid-but-not-special passer who produced positive EPA (around +0.09 to +0.10 per play in each of his first two years) and added 356 to 430 rushing yards a season as a real second threat. Five games into 2026, the passing efficiency has gone negative at -0.053 per dropback, 29th of 43. His 5.81 yards per attempt is 38th. The rushing is nearly gone: 35 yards on 18 carries, 7 a game, after roughly 21 to 25 a game in his first two seasons. Only four of his 174 dropbacks became scrambles. That is the biggest single change in his profile, and nothing in the dossier explains it. He is healthy and has started every snap, so it reads as a choice, either his or Payton's.

The offense has been shrunk down to keep him safe. Forty-three of his 162 attempts (about 26%) have been thrown behind the line of scrimmage, and those plays return -0.327 EPA. The average throw lands 3 yards short of the sticks. That shows up on third down, where he faces 7.5 yards to go on average and converts just 26.5%. Between 10 and 19 air yards he completes 41.7%, with a CPOE of -12.9 and two of his three picks. Over the middle he is 33% on 15 throws. What does work is the plain quick game. Throws of 0 to 9 yards carry +0.104 EPA and a 47% success rate. He is also efficient in the red zone, with all six of his touchdowns coming from 26 plays there.

The protection numbers hide part of the problem. He has the 5th-lowest sack rate, and the offense allows the fewest QB hits in the league. That is partly the line and partly the quick-game menu. It is also why his 15.4% bad-throw rate (29th of 36) and -4.07 tracked CPOE stand out: he is missing throws from clean pockets. The receiver room hasn't helped. Courtland Sutton is at -0.428 EPA per target on 25 looks. Pat Bryant was the most efficient target on the team at +0.95 per target, and he just went to IR until early November. The few deep shots have been good (+0.437 EPA on 12 attempts), but 12 throws is a hint, not a skill shift.

The Broncos are 3-2 because their defense ranks 7th in EPA and 3rd against the pass, not because of their quarterback. As long as that holds, Denver can win low-scoring games with Nix as a caretaker. Getting back to his 2024-25 level probably needs two things: the rushing returning, and the intermediate throws starting to connect. Until one of them does, expect roughly 13 PPR points a week.

strengths.title: Clean pockets, very few sacks
strengths.body: He takes a sack on just 3.6% of dropbacks and converts only 15.6% of pressures into sacks. Protection is part of it: Denver allows the fewest QB hits in the league. The quick-game menu is the other part. Low pressure-to-sack rates held in both prior seasons, so this is stable. The catch is that some of it is bought with very short throws.

strengths.title: Short game and red-zone finishing
strengths.body: Throws of 0 to 9 air yards are the one high-volume area producing positive EPA, with a 47% success rate and 4 TDs. Inside the 20 he has been efficient, with all six passing scores. The short-area efficiency is real and repeatable. A 6-for-6 red-zone TD share on 26 plays is the kind of number that drifts back.

concerns.title: Screen-heavy offense that can't reach sticks
concerns.body: A quarter of his attempts go behind the line at -0.327 EPA. His average throw lands 3 yards short of the sticks, which is why third down has been a dead end. This is mostly scheme and caution rather than a sudden skill loss: his aDOT was 7.4 to 7.5 in prior years. It does cap the offense until the intermediate game opens up.

concerns.title: Intermediate accuracy has cratered
concerns.body: From 10 to 19 yards he completes 41.7%, with a CPOE of -12.9 and two interceptions on 24 throws. Combined with a bottom-tier bad-throw rate from mostly clean pockets, this looks like a real accuracy problem rather than pressure. It is a small sample, but his CPOE was already below average last year, so there is history behind it.

concerns.title: The rushing floor is gone
concerns.body: He has 35 yards on 18 carries after 430 and 356 the past two seasons, and he has scrambled just four times. Designed runs are still efficient near the goal line (+0.379 EPA). As a yardage source, though, his legs have vanished, along with the fantasy floor they gave him. Add 2 lost fumbles on 5 turnover-worthy fumbles, and the ball security around the pocket needs watching.

trend.note: Game-by-game pass EPA has swung from -14.4 to +8.4 to -1.1 to +4.7 to -6.5 with no direction. His best efficiency came against top defenses (JAX, SF), and his worst came in two division games.

nextGame.headline: Short week, a top-two defense, and his best target on IR
nextGame.body:
Seattle's defense ranks 2nd in overall EPA, pass EPA, rush EPA and success rate. It also allows the fewest passing yards a game to quarterbacks (189). It is 2nd in explosive pass rate and 3rd in deep EPA, which takes away the small deep sample that has flattered Nix. The one opening fits his game. Seattle ranks 25th in EPA on short throws, right where Nix lives when he isn't throwing screens. WR1s have also done well against this defense (+0.46 EPA per target, 24th), which points to Jaylen Waddle. Seattle's 2nd-ranked rush defense means there's no relief from his rushing either.

Availability matters on both sides. Bryant's move to IR removes Nix's most efficient target and his WR3 snaps, though Seattle has smothered WR3s anyway. That pushes more volume to Waddle and to Sutton, who has been a drag. For Seattle, LB Drake Thomas (87% of snaps) didn't practice Monday. Losing him would soften the short middle, where Nix has been poor. DT Leonard Williams is also questionable. On offense, QB Drew Lock is limited with a forearm injury, Smith-Njigba is questionable and Charbonnet is out. That leaves Seattle's 26th-ranked offense weaker still against Denver's top-three pass defense. This is a Thursday game on four days' rest.

keyMatchups.title: Quick game vs Seattle's soft underneath
keyMatchups.body: Seattle bleeds EPA on short throws even while dominating everywhere else, and Nix's 0-9 yard throws are his most productive area. If Thomas sits, the underneath zones get softer still. Expect the plan to lean on high-percentage throws at or just past the line.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots into a wall
keyMatchups.body: His 12 deep attempts have been his best-per-play throws. Seattle allows the 2nd-lowest explosive pass rate and the 3rd-best deep EPA, so the one thing that has broken open games for him is the area Seattle shuts down best.

keyMatchups.title: Waddle as WR1 vs Seattle
keyMatchups.body: Waddle leads the team in targets with positive EPA per target. Seattle has given WR1s more than their usual output. With Bryant out, Waddle is the most logical path to Nix's yardage.

nextGame.watch: Whether Denver throws on early downs at least 10 yards past the line. If the screens and sub-sticks throws continue against this defense, third downs will stall again.

restOfSeason.body:
The low sack rate, the efficient short game and Denver's defense keeping games close look sustainable. Those are the base: about 180 to 230 passing yards and one-plus touchdown in most weeks. The red-zone touchdown efficiency should cool, and the deep-ball EPA on 12 attempts will not stay at +0.44. Losing Bryant until November removes the target who made the quick game pop.

The upside path is the rushing. His two-year history says it is a real skill, and even a partial return of 15 to 20 yards a game would lift both his efficiency and his weekly floor. Absent that, he is a mid-pack starter on a defense-led team. His 2025 profile of weak CPOE but positive EPA suggests some bounce in yards per attempt is plausible once the screen rate falls.
swingFactors: Whether the designed and scramble rushing returns
Intermediate accuracy and a lower screen rate

bets.reason: Two top-seven defenses meet two bottom-nine offenses (DEN 24th, SEA 26th in EPA) on a Thursday short week. Denver has gone under in 4 of 5 games, and Seattle's QB Lock and WR Smith-Njigba are both limited.

He hasn't topped 10 rushing yards in any game this season (7 a game) and has scrambled four times. Seattle ranks 2nd in rush EPA allowed, so a line shaded toward his 21-25 yard career pace looks too high.

Seattle allows the fewest passing yards to QBs and the 2nd-lowest explosive pass rate, which takes away his deep throws. A screen-heavy plan with Bryant on IR limits his ceiling, though the soft short zone keeps this from being a stronger call.

In a projected low total, 2.5 points carries weight. Denver is at home with the 3rd-ranked pass defense facing a Seattle offense that ranks 30th in rush EPA and has a limited QB. Denver has covered 3 of 5.

confidence.note: Five games of clear decline from a two-year baseline, but split samples (deep, middle, red zone) are small.
